{"id": "oil-ground", "title": "Oil ground handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Ground

- An **oil ground** (the default) absorbs nothing: paint stays open and
  glossy longer. An **absorbent ground** (`absorbent=true`) drinks the oil of
  thin paint: matte, lean, quick to set, colors that sit on the surface;
  thick paint is barely touched. Choose before you start: it is the
  canvas's character.
- A **toned ground** (a little ochre, umber or black in the white) sets the
  middle value from the first stroke; a white ground keeps everything high
  in key and lets thin paint glow.
"}

{"id": "oil-spatter", "title": "Oil spatter at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Spatter

- **Flicked paint makes scattered marks.**
  `b:spatter{at={x, y}, toward={dx, dy}}` throws droplets whose sizes,
  spacing and colors vary by themselves: aim the flick and let the droplets
  fall.
- **Thin the paint to make it fly**: a pile with medium or turpentine
  spatters; blotted paint hardly does. A hard flick gives a fine spray, a
  gentle one fat drops.
- **Mask what must stay clean** with `clip=`: droplets fly past any edge.
- A few flicks over a passage, then look.
"}

{"id": "oil-impasto", "title": "Impasto handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "- Stiff paint holds the brush's marks: blot it (`pile{..., blot=0.3}`) or
  use it as it comes from the tube, with no medium. A full brush lays more with `lay=4`
  to `lay=16`; a coarse hog brush (larger `hair`) leaves coarser ridges.
- In stiff paint the hairs gather into clumps: strokes lie in ridges and
  furrows, walls rise along their sides, a bead where they end. Fluid paint
  levels flat, which suits a glaze.
- Check it with `look` and `mode: "relief"` (raking light from the upper
  left at 25°: it exaggerates, as a raking lamp does) and with
  `mode: "gallery"` (55°, as the picture is seen on a wall). Judge the
  picture under the gallery light; use raking light to inspect the surface.
- Let impasto set before painting into it, unless you want the new stroke
  to drag the old one along.
"}

{"id": "oil-glazes", "title": "Glazing and scumbling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Glazing and scumbling (over dry paint)

- **Glaze**: a transparent paint (lakes, viridian, ultramarine, a little of
  anything) with plenty of medium (0.7 to 0.85), `hand="glaze"`, over a dry
  passage. It deepens and saturates and lets the light underneath through;
  it rescues a chalky passage. Over impasto it pools in the valleys and
  thins on the ridges, which then shine through. Too much pigment, or any
  white, lays an opaque veil: try it small first. A glaze over the whole
  picture to pull it together has failed more often than it has worked.
- **Scumble**: light paint dragged thin over a dry darker passage, broken
  by the surface. A light load and
  `hand="scumble"` often lay opaque dabs. The veils that blended in came
  from paint thinned with `thinner`, laid in several light passes. Try it
  on the scratch canvas first.
- Glazes and scumbles want the passage under them **dry** (`wait` until
  `drying` says so): over open paint they just mix.
"}

{"id": "oil-blending", "title": "Blending at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Blending

- **Blend inside one passage.** Shape the mask like the passage, with its
  edge where the paint already matches. Keep everything you want to keep
  outside the mask, dry shapes included: the blender carries wet paint onto
  them.
- **Look after each pass.** The blender lifts paint as it moves it. When
  darks go pale, texture flattens or the weave shows through, stop.
- **A seam that keeps coming back** needs another method. A smaller patch
  blended again rebuilds the box. Try something else across the whole
  transition on the scratch canvas: a thin tint of the original recipe,
  interlocking strokes of the two neighboring colors over dry paint, or the
  connected passage repainted up to its natural edges.
"}

{"id": "oil-rag-time", "title": "Rag handling and drying time at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## The rag

- **It lifts wet paint down to the first set layer.** Earlier passes that
  haven't set are part of the same wet film, so a firm lift can take them
  too, down to set paint or the ground. Before a wipe, check
  `drying(x, y)` in the paint: `"open"` paint lifts, `"setting"` paint
  comes away slowly, and `"tacky"` or `"dry"` paint has set and stays.
  A wipe usually leaves a thin wet tint, and `drying(x, y)` reads that
  tint as `"open"` or `"setting"`. If the tint is `"setting"`, or the set
  layer under it is still tacky, it grabs the brush when you repaint.
  Check it at a nearby gap in the paint, where `drying(x, y)` reads the
  set layer.
- **Dip it for a lift.** A dry rag mostly moves paint and leaves its color
  in the weave: useful for wiping lights out of a wet glaze or lay-in. To
  take a passage off, dip well (`r:dip(0.9)`), press firmly, give it two or
  three passes, then go over it again across the first direction with a
  fresh, dipped rag.
- **The spirits go in minutes.** Dampness halves every three minutes of
  painting time, and a long mask wipe takes minutes. Dip just before each
  wipe; `print(r.damp)` says how much is left.
- **A loaded face puts paint back.** `print(r.load)`: near 1, the face
  lifts little and smears. Refold (`refold=` in a mask wipe) or take a
  fresh rag.
- **The rag runs past the mask.** Its rim reaches past the mask's edge and
  lays lifted paint on what is next to it, dry shapes included. Keep the
  mask clear of edges you need crisp. Along an edge, wipe a path parallel
  to it with a rag narrower than the strip.
- **Shape the mask like the passage.** Mask wipes start and stop a little
  inside the mask, so a rectangle leaves a frame of the wiped color. If a
  frame shows, wipe along its sides with a path.
- **Expect a trace.** Even a good lift leaves a tint, streaks along the
  wipe or a rim where it stopped. Look at a detail crop before you call it
  clean, and before you paint over it. Thick paint takes many fresh, dipped
  wipes.
- **One lift, then a new plan.** If the same passage needs lifting twice,
  change what goes on it before painting it again.

## Time

- Time passes only as you paint or `wait`. Paint dries on its own clock:
  lead white and umber fast, lakes and vermilion slow, thin paint faster than
  thick. Added medium and the slower oils (walnut, poppy) slow it; an
  absorbent ground sets thin paint laid straight on it quickly.
- **Check `drying(x, y)` at several points** along the next pass, its edges
  included: thick and thin parts of one passage dry at different rates.
- A painting can take months of painted time. Let layers dry between
  campaigns; that is what lets the next one sit on top.
"}

{"id": "pigments", "title": "Pigment behavior and documented estimates", "page": 1, "pages": 4, "next_page": 2, "text": "**Terms.** *Masstone*: the color of the paint laid thick. *Hiding*: how
much one coat covers what is under it. *Tinting strength*: how far a
pigment carries its color into a mixture. *Lake*: a dye fixed on a
colorless base, a transparent pigment. *Glaze*: a transparent layer.
*Scumble*: a thin, semi-opaque layer dragged over dry paint. *Ground*: the
preparatory layer between canvas and paint. *Traction crackle*: wide
cracks where a layer shrinks over paint that was not yet dry. *Fugitive*:
fading in light.

## 4. The paints in the box

### Whites

- **lead white** (basic lead carbonate). Lead "produces a uniquely strong
  paint film, and dries rapidly"; lead white is a rapid dryer. Period tube paints held "linseed oil in the darker colours and
  poppyseed oil in white paint". It is the
  white of documented grounds: gray grounds of lead white and ivory black
  in linseed oil, lead white with calcite
  and a little black, or pink with red iron oxide. Documented as a final scumble over toning layers.
  Aged films: lead white shrank 0.5% over 21–31 years, and its strain at
  break fell from 7.3% at 0.2 years to under 1%. Lead-soap
  protrusions can form in a lead-white ground.
- **zinc white** (zinc oxide). In oil it "tends … to form hard, often
  brittle films" that crack over softer layers. Aged zinc white
  films break at 0.1–0.3% strain, the most brittle white measured; it
  forms brittle soaps with the oil. A canvas of 1935 whose paint
  included zinc white shows old flaking, fractures through and between
  layers and zinc soaps. *Uncertain* (read through a summary). Period
  tube colors sometimes held a little zinc white inside them.

### Yellows

- **chrome yellow** (lead chromate). Made commercially in Germany only from
  1820. It darkens with age. A manual of
  1887 rejects it: "its stability is too doubtful". With
  Prussian blue it makes chrome green; with
  cobalt blue it gives greens too.
- **lemon chrome** (pale lead chromate with lead sulfate). The pale grade
  is coprecipitated with lead sulfate, which makes it hide and
  tint less than chrome yellow. A "pale lemon chrome" was in a
  paint box of about 1884–88.
- **strontium yellow** (strontium chromate). A lead-free chromate yellow of
  the 1850s–80s; measured as a dry powder, it tints at about 78% of lead
  chromate. Found in French paint of the 1880s.
- **barium yellow** (barium chromate, "lemon yellow"). Measured as a dry
  powder, it tints at about 92% of lead chromate. It turns green with
  age. Documented used together with zinc yellow.
- **zinc yellow** (potassium zinc chromate). Measured as a dry powder, it
  tints at about 65% of lead chromate. It browns or turns green with
  age, to a dichromate brown or a chromium-oxide green.
- **lead-tin yellow** (lead-tin oxide). Its hiding, body and drying in the
  catalog are sourced: an opaque, stiff paint that dries
  at lead white's rate. Modern tubes of this name vary.
- **Naples yellow** (lead antimonate). "In use since antiquity until about
  1850"; what a later tube of this name held is *unverified*. A lead
  compound; its drying between average and lead white's is an estimate. Documented in green mixtures with blues.
- **pale cadmium**, **cadmium yellow** and **deep cadmium** (cadmium
  sulfide in three grades). Cadmium pigments were in use "since about 1840" and sold in England by 1846; the names ran from pale
  yellow to "orange" for the darker shades. "Good hiding power"; one maker rates it opaque. The cadmiums are "slow but
  reliable driers". Documented as a scumbling color.
  Emerald green blackens with cadmium sulfide. Deep cadmium's hue (a
  deep yellow or orange) is *inferred*.
- **Indian yellow** (magnesium and calcium euxanthate). Its particles are
  "uniformly clear and transparent". An early account has it
  drying in oil "nearly as soon or sooner than" other colors.
  *Uncertain.* Sold as "genuine Indian yellow" in the 1880s.
- **yellow lake** (flavonoid dye, such as weld or quercit"}

{"id": "oil-loading", "title": "Uneven paint loading at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "- **Two colors on one brush.** `b:load(p, 0.8); b:load(p2, 0.5, {side=1, share=0.4})`, or
  `work(m, {pile=p, second={pile=p2, side=1, share=0.45}})`: each stroke carries both,
  side by side, mingling as it goes. `streak=` loads unevenly, in bands.
- **Wet into wet.** A stroke dragged through wet paint picks some of it up
  and carries it along: color changes within the stroke. Work an area while
  it is open (`drying(x, y)` says "open") for soft transitions; wait for it
  to set for crisp, separate strokes on top.
"}

{"id": "optical-mixing", "title": "Optical mixing and simultaneous contrast", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "**Optical mixing is not emitted-light mixing.** Adjacent touches remain actual
pigmented paint. At a distance their reflected colors integrate, while
simultaneous contrast can intensify their appearance where they remain resolved.
Very small complementary dots can also average toward gray; the technical
authors explicitly note the difference between the theory's promise and the
paintings' effect. Do not simulate this by RGB gradients
or promise that blue and yellow dots necessarily become a brilliant green.
"}

{"id": "oil-knife", "title": "Knife handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## The knife

- `k = knife{width=30}; k:load(p, 1.0); k:lay(points, {pressure={0.5, 0.5}})`
  lays a slab with a flat top, torn where it parts from the blade (its ends,
  its leading edge): light pressure lays it thick, and the paint runs out
  sooner; firm pressure thin, and it goes further. The points set its path.
- Pulled lightly over **dry** impasto, it catches only the ridges: broken
  color over a textured underlayer, a sparkle of light paint on dark.
- `k:scrape(points, {pressure=1})` takes wet paint off down to what is dry:
  to restate a passage, or to leave a ghost of it.
"}

function flash_trial(cx, cy, variant)
  local b = brush{kind="filbert", width=10, stiffness=0.5}
  -- outer glow: radial strokes, thinned orange
  b:load(glow_o, 0.6)

  b2:load(glow_y, 0.8)

content.thinking:
This is reading as a cartoon star rather than a muzzle flash—the thinned radial strokes create a scratchy, dry-brush texture that breaks over the canvas weave into a speckled veil instead of a glow. The yellow spikes look too regular and cartoonish, and the white core is too small to read as luminous.

What would actually sell a muzzle flash? Thinking of Western painters like Frank McCarthy, Lovell, Wyeth—it should be an irregular burst of yellow-white fire with flame tongues pushing forward, plus a billowing cloud of black-powder smoke lit orange-yellow from within and fading to gray-white at its edges against the dark sky. The flash itself needs a white-yellow core with orange edges and sparks of burning powder spraying forward like spatter. So I'm breaking it into layered elements: first a soft, irregular billowing smoke cloud.

I'm sizing and positioning the smoke mass roughly 100x70 units from the muzzle forward/upward, warm and lit at its center but cooling to gray-blue-white moonlit tones at the edges, blending softly into the sky. Then a jagged flame tongue extending 60-80 units with a white-yellow core and ragged orange-red edges, sparks spattering forward in orange-yellow droplets, and small side jets of flare at the cylinder gap. For the soft glow around it all, I'm thinking of blending wet-into-wet in paint—laying warm transitional tones around the flash and blending them into the surrounding sky. I'm sketching out a layered approach: a rough-edged smoke blob built from graded piles of color, warm lead white mixed with Naples and cad yellow at center, shifting to yellow ochre and orange in the middle tones, then cooling to lead white with bone black and Prussian blue at the outer edges.

That thinned scumble is actually just producing a grainy weave texture with hard edges, like a fabric patch rather than soft smoke—and the flame reads as a cartoon shape instead. So I'm learning that thinning the scumble too much just catches on the weave tops instead of creating a soft veil, and the lost edge trick isn't softening things the way I need.

For smoke, I should work wet-in-wet instead: repaint the sky area fresh, then while it's still wet, paint the smoke and warm glow directly into it and blend so the edges actually fuse together, the way clouds are traditionally handled. I'll test this on scratch paper first—fresh wet sky patch, then undiluted smoke paint blended in lightly.

The flame needs rethinking too: instead of separate spikes, I want broad irregular flame-like tongues blended softly into the glow, with an elongated white-yellow teardrop core at the muzzle, a yellow-orange cone around it, and a few ragged orange tongues extending outward.

For the glow itself, I'm wary that mixing orange with blue sky paint will just turn muddy gray-green rather than reading as light—so instead I'll paint the glow opaquely with warm lead white, yellow, and orange, and let the blend zone toward the blue sky go slightly gray, which actually works fine since smoke is grayish anyway. I'll test this by laying a fresh wet sky rectangle in that region before adding the flame and smoke.

content.thinking:
Looking at the overall composition, I notice the figures read as flat silhouettes, the moon's salmon color feels off since the paper ground still shows through, and the glow looks too much like a circular second moon rather than a directional blast. I'm also thinking the ground tone is too light compared to the sky, even though the foreground shading works well. The main fix needed is reshaping the glow into a forward-directed cone of flame with smoke expanding to the sides, rather than a uniform circle.

I need to work on modeling the figures with warm flash-light on their front-facing sides (cowboy's gun arm and face, zombie's front and arms) and cool moon-rim light elsewhere, paint the moon itself properly, add spatter and grave details, and establish a warm light pool on the ground beneath the flash. The zombie's arms also need better anatomy—claws, elbows, tattered sleeves—instead of reading as noodles, and I'm noting the gun barrel position relative to where the flash should actually originate. I'm pleased that the flash sits centrally between the two figures, which works well for the story the image tells. Now I'm moving into mixing the moon's paint color using lead white, Naples yellow, and a touch of ochre, with gray for the maria, followed by building a soft halo around it.

I'm figuring out where the warm ground pool from the flash should land—roughly between the figures near their feet—and sizing it as a broad, faint ellipse. I also need to account for two separate shadow sources: the flash throwing shadows behind each figure, and the moonlight from upper right casting a second set of shadows toward the lower-left, toward the viewer, since the moon sits beyond the figures in the scene. Before adding the ground light though, I'm checking the drying status of the ground paint in the foreground, since parts are still tacky and need more time.

Now I'm working out the figure lighting itself—the cowboy's dry, flat form needs highlights where the flash hits: the gun hand brightest, then the forearm underside, the front of the face and hat brim, the chest and coat edges, fading in intensity with distance from the flash. I'm also planning a faint rim light from the moon behind the scene, catching the top of the hat crown and shoulders.

For the zombie, the flash comes from the left, so I'll light the chin and throat (head tilted back), the chest front, the arm undersides, and especially the near hand. The moon will rim the back of the head, shoulder, and coat on the opposite side, giving both figures depth instead of flat silhouettes.

Now I'm thinking through the internal costume details each figure needs—the cowboy with his hat, bandana, vest, gun belt, chaps, and duster, versus the zombie with gray-green decaying skin, tattered burial suit, torn shirt, and sunken-eyed, open-mouthed face with stringy hair. I'm planning to block in these elements first using dark but distinct base colors (brown-black coat, dark trousers, ruddy shadowed face for the cowboy; bluish-black suit and green-gray skin for the zombie) before letting the flash and moonlight carve out the highlights.

I'm working out how to render the lit planes where flash light hits each form—trying to figure out a way to generate lit bands along the edges of each part facing the light source, considering whether I can approximate this with some kind of shape offsetting technique rather than building full 3D geometry.

Actually, I think the cleaner approach is to just hand-draw the lit edges directly as gestural shapes for the key figures (face, hand, gun) rather than trying to mechanically derive them from offset operations, and treat larger surfaces similarly.

Before continuing with figures, I want to fix the moon and reassess the ground value—right now the ground near the horizon reads too close to the sky's value, and I'd rather have the sky glow more there while the ground stays a touch darker. Let me check the value squint again before glazing it down.

function rimw(M, ux, uy, depth)
  return function(x,y)

function rimdir(M, tx, ty, depths)
  return function(x,y)
    if M:at(x,y) < 0.5 then return 0 end
    local dx, dy = tx - x, ty - y
    local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); dx, dy = dx/d, dy/d
    local s = 0
    for _, k in ipairs(depths) do s = s + (1 - M:at(x+dx*k, y+dy*k)) end
    return s/#depths
  end
end

function cross(x, base, h, lean, wbar, pw)
  local top = {x + math.sin(lean)*h, base - math.cos(lean)*h}
  local post = ribbon({{x, base+2}, {top[1], top[2]}}, pw)
  local by = 0.72
  local bc = {x + math.sin(lean)*h*by, base - math.cos(lean)*h*by}
  local ca, sa = math.cos(lean), math.sin(lean)
  local tilt = rand(-0.08, 0.08)
  local bar = ribbon({{bc[1]-ca*wbar/2, bc[2]-sa*wbar/2 + tilt*wbar}, {bc[1]+ca*wbar/2, bc[2]+sa*wbar/2 - tilt*wbar}}, pw*0.85)
  local m = (post + bar)
  work(m, {hand="detail", tool={kind="flat", width=math.max(2, pw*0.7)}, pile=wood_d, coverage=3, fill=true, clip=true, length={4,10}, angle=-1.57+lean})
  -- moonlit right edge
  local edge = m - m:offset(-1.2):shrink(0) 
  local lit = m * (m:offset(-0.1) - m:shrink(1.3)) * mask(function(px,py) return (1 - m:at(px+1.8, py-0.7)) end)
  work(lit, {hand="detail", tool={kind="round", width=1.2}, pile=wood_l, coverage=2, fill=true, clip=true, length={3,8}, angle=-1.57+lean})
  return m
end

local function off(p, d)
  local o = {}
  for i = 1, #p do
    local a = p[math.max(1,i-1)]; local b = p[math.min(#p,i+1)]
    local tx, ty = b[1]-a[1], b[2]-a[2]; local L = math.sqrt(tx*tx+ty*ty)

end

  local m = ellipse(cx, cy - h*0.45, w*0.5, h*0.55):roughen(w*0.12, w*0.3, seed):soften(1.5) * above({{0,cy},{1000,cy}})
  stipple(m, {pile=sage_d, width=w*0.12, coverage=2.2, cluster=0.5, pressure={0.4,0.8}, seed=seed})
  -- moonlit top-right
  local top = m * mask(function(x,y) return clamp(((x-cx)/w*0.8 - (y-(cy-h*0.6))/h) , 0, 1) end)
  stipple(top, {pile=sage_l, width=w*0.08, coverage=0.7, cluster=0.6, pressure={0.3,0.6}, feather=0.5, seed=seed+1})
  -- a few stems at the base
  local r = brush{kind="round", width=1.4, point=0.8}
  r:load(sage_d, 0.6)
  for i = 1, 3 do
    local x0 = cx + rand(-w*0.15, w*0.15)
    r:gesture({{x0, cy+1, 0.7},{x0 + rand(-3,3), cy - h*0.25, 0.3}})
  end
  return m
end

arguments.text:
## Finish (day 154) — reflections & handoff
Title: "Boot Hill, Midnight". Finished: moonlit nocturne, gunslinger left firing, muzzle flame + lit powder cloud center, skull-faced zombie right with its head snapped back and a dark spray toward the moon, Boot Hill crosses, distant mesa. Signed lower right ("Cl", red earth/ochre rigger). All dry at day 154.
Unresolved / accepted:
- Cowboy's coat is a flat dark mass: fold trials (glaze gestures, ribbon glazes, blend) never read as cloth; accepted as silhouette. A thin cool rim and the warm sleeve/hand carry it.
- Zombie torso is a flat dark wedge with a pale shirt stripe; legs are plain dark columns.
- The powder cloud is a little hard-edged and cotton-ball-like; moon and cloud both near-white, so they compete slightly.
- Sky left/top keeps faint patches from repainting around changed silhouettes.
Practical lessons (carry forward; rules are hypotheses):
1. ~10-15% lead white lifts dark umber/black mixes to mid value: keep night darks at <=4% white.
2. body/broad strokes overrun their masks by up to a stroke length: always clip= when painting AROUND a shape.
3. A big radial glow reads as a second moon; a gunshot reads as flame jet + lumpy smoke lit from inside + warm edges on the figures.
4. Spirits rag on small FRESH passages over DRY paint smears them around; knife scrape (width 10-14, pressure 1, crossing passes) while open is cleaner. Over fresh paint down to the ground, the rag exposes the pale ground.
5. Small dark features (eyes, mouths) are best as filled polygons over a dry base, with no blending after.
6. Thin dark rigger strokes over light sky read as insect legs; make extremities part of the silhouette masks.
7. Repeated sky repaints around changed silhouettes leave ridges/ghosts; cover by changing the silhouette or folding into a cloud.
8. Glaze cglaze (bone black .6/umber .8/ultramarine .3, medium .78) over dry paint = clean one-step darkening; zglaze similar with green earth for the zombie. Sky glaze with medium .82 showed dark veining in scratch.
9. Thick white-heavy glow mixes stay open ~3 days and tacky ~6; flame over the glow only once dry.

content.text:
**Boot Hill, Midnight**

This is a moonlit nocturne in blues and greens. A gunslinger in a long duster stands on the left, arm straight out. His Colt fires a yellow-white flame into a billowing cloud of powder smoke, lit from inside, and that is the only hot color in the picture. On the right, a skull-faced zombie in a rotting burial coat reaches toward him with bony claws. Its head is snapped back with the jaw open, and a dark spray flies off toward the full moon. The crosses of Boot Hill sit on the rise behind it, a blue mesa lies on the horizon, and the flash leaves a dull warm glow on the sand between the two figures. The picture is signed lower right and was fully dry by day 154 of painting time.

**Still unresolved:**
- **The cowboy's coat** stays a flat dark mass. None of my scratch trials for folds read as cloth, so I left it as a silhouette.
- **The zombie's torso and legs** are fairly plain dark shapes.
- **The smoke cloud** is a bit like a cotton ball. Being nearly as pale as the moon, the two compete slightly.
- **The sky behind the cowboy's hat** still shows faint patches from repainting it around his changing outline.

**Lessons to carry forward (general rules are still hypotheses):**
- **Not much white turns darks to middle values.** In these dark mixes, 10–15% lead white made them mid-tones; I kept night darks at 4% or less.
- **Brush passes run past their mask** by up to a stroke's length. When painting around a shape, always clip to the area being covered. Not doing this once buried the whole flash.
- **A big round glow looks like a second moon.** The shot finally read once I painted a flame, a lumpy smoke cloud lit from inside, and warm edges on the figures.
- **Rag lifts went wrong.** On small fresh passages over dry paint, the rag smeared the paint around. Where the fresh paint went down to the ground, it exposed the pale ground. Scraping with the knife while the paint was still open was cleaner.
- **Small dark features** (eye sockets, mouth) worked best as filled shapes painted over a dry base, with no blending afterwards.
- **Repainting sky around a changed outline** kept leaving ridges. It worked better to change the outline to cover the ghost, or to turn the patch into a cloud.
- **The dark glaze for shadows** (bone black, raw umber and ultramarine in about 78% medium) darkened dry paint by about one value step, cleanly. A similar glaze tried on the sky in scratch showed dark veins, so I didn't use it there.
